topics.title: Instruction Codes
notes: An instruction code is a group of bits that tells the computer to perform a specific operation. Each computer has its own instruction code format.
An instruction is divided into two parts: Opcode (operation code, says what to do) and Operand (data or address on which the operation is performed).
Opcode is a group of bits for basic operations like add, subtract, multiply, shift and complement. Its size depends on the number of operations: 64 operations need 6 bits (2^6 = 64).
Operand is the data (or address of data) used by the operation. Example: in 2 + 3, the numbers 2 and 3 are operands.
Instruction example from the slide: ADD 101 301 -> opcode ADD (operation), operands 101 and 301 (data/addresses).
Opcode is a unique binary code for each operation. It cannot be changed and is fixed when the computer is designed.

topics.title: Processor Registers & Basic Computer Architecture
notes: A basic computer needs certain registers: PC (Program Counter, 12 bits) holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched; AR (Address Register, 12 bits, also MAR) holds the address of the memory location to be accessed; IR (Instruction Register, 16 bits) holds the instruction being executed; DR/MDR (Data Register, 16 bits) holds memory operands fetched from memory; TR (Temporary Register, 16 bits) holds temporary data during processing.
AC (Accumulator, 16 bits) is the processor register that holds intermediate and final results of arithmetic and logic operations and performs micro-operations.
INPR (Input Register, 8 bits) holds the input characters given by the user. OUTR (Output Register, 8 bits) holds the output characters to send to the output device.
Memory of the basic computer: 4096 words x 16 bits each (4096 = 2^12, so 12-bit addresses).
A bus is a wire or collection of wires that carries multi-bit information from one unit to another.
Three control signals used on register: LD (load, copies data from bus into register), INR (increment content), CLR (clear content to zero).
PC increments automatically after each fetch, so instructions are read in sequence.
Slide conflict: the general register slide says CPU generally has 7 registers, but the bus slide shows 8 registers in the basic computer (PC, AR, IR, TR, DR, AC, INPR, OUTR). Use the bus-slide list.

topics.title: Common Bus System
notes: In a common bus system, all registers are connected to one shared bus. Only one register can place its data on the bus at a time.
Select lines S2, S1, S0 (3 bits) choose which register drives the bus: 8 registers can be selected with 3 select lines.
The register whose LD input is enabled receives the data from the bus.
ALU can receive data from DR, INPR or AC, and sends the result to AC. When the result is produced, it can be sent to OUTR for output.

topics.title: Micro-operations & Control Word
notes: Micro-operations are basic operations performed on data stored in registers, such as transfer, increment, decrement, AND, OR, XOR, complement, shift right and shift left.
Example operation codes: 00000 Transfer A, 00001 Increment A, 00100 Decrement A, 00101 A AND B, 00110 A OR B, 00111 A XOR B, 01000 Complement A, 01001 Shift right A, 01010 Shift left A.
Control word = SELA (3 bits) + SELB (3 bits) + SELD/SELREG (3 bits) + SELOPR (5 bits) = 14 bits (as on the slide: 3, 3, 5, 3). Operation codes like 10010 are 5 bits.
Example: R3 = R1 + R2 uses SELA = 001 (R1 on bus A), SELB = 010 (R2 on bus B), SELOPR = 10010 (ADD A+B), SELD = 011 (result into R3).

topics.title: Stack Organization
notes: A stack is a data structure in which the item stored last is the first item retrieved (LIFO: Last In First Out).
Two operations: PUSH (insert an item on the top of the stack) and POP (remove or retrieve the item from the top).
A stack can be a separate unit, or it can be placed in a portion of a large random-access memory using a processor register as a stack pointer (SP).
SP (Stack Pointer) is a register that holds the address of the item on top of the stack.
PUSH steps: SP <- SP + 1; M[SP] <- DR; if SP = 0 then stack is FULL. POP steps: DR <- M[SP]; SP <- SP - 1; if SP = 0 then stack is EMPTY.
Computer memory is partitioned into three segments: Program (instructions), Data (operands) and Stack.
Stacks are used in expression evaluation, and Reverse Polish Notation (RPN, postfix) works well with a stack. Example: 3 4 * 5 6 * + = (3x4) + (5x6) = 12 + 30 = 42.
Memory stack example (slide): program segment at 1000, operands at 2000, stack at 3000. PC points to program, AR to operands, SP to stack.
PUSH flags: if SP = 0 then FULL = 1 (and EMPTY = 0). POP flags: if SP = 0 then EMPTY = 1 (and FULL = 0).
Infix to postfix: A*B + C*D becomes AB* CD* +.

topics.title: Instruction Formats
notes: Three address format: instruction has three operands (e.g. X = A + B needs 3 addresses). Uses more bits per instruction but gives shorter programs in assembly.
Two address format: instruction has two address fields. It is the most commonly used format. Example: (A+B)*(C+D) can be done with two-address moves and operations.
One address format: one operand is in the accumulator (AC) and the other is in memory. Uses special instructions LOAD and STORE.
Zero address format: no address field. Stack is used for operands, so it is also called stack-based format. Example: PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD.
Three-address example: (A+B)*(C+D) = ADD R1,A,B; ADD R2,C,D; MUL X,R1,R2.
Two-address example: MOV R1,A; ADD R1,B; MOV R2,C; ADD R2,D; MUL R1,R2; MOV X,R1.
One-address example: LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X.

topics.title: Addressing Modes
notes: Addressing mode = the technique for specifying the address of the operand.
Direct (absolute) addressing: address field contains the effective address of the operand. Example: ADD 547 adds the content of memory location 547 to AC.

Indirect addressing: address field points to a memory word that contains the address of the operand. Example: ADD 300 means memory[300] holds the address of the operand. Two memory references are needed.
Immediate addressing: operand itself is given in the instruction (no memory reference is needed).
Register (direct) addressing: operand is in a CPU register. No memory reference is required. Example: ADD R adds the content of register R to AC.
Register indirect addressing: the register holds the address of the operand in memory. Only one memory reference is required.
Implied addressing: operand is implied by the instruction. Example: CMA (Complement Accumulator). Zero address instructions in a stack computer are implied mode instructions.
Auto-decrement / auto-increment: register is decremented or incremented automatically when used to access memory.
Direct example: instruction at address 20 is ADD 547, so the operand is read from memory location 547.
Indirect example: ADD 300 at address 35. Memory[300] = 1350, so the operand is at 1350.
Immediate example: ADD 10 means add the value 10 itself.
Register mode: AC <- AC + [R]. Register indirect: AC <- AC + [[R]] (the register holds the address, memory holds the operand).
Auto-decrement: the register pointer is decremented first and then used to access memory (slide example: 3302 -> 3300).
Implied mode examples from the slide: SWAPA and RLA (operand is implied by the instruction).

mcq.q: In an instruction code, the part that specifies the operation to be performed is called:
mcq.explanation: Opcode = operation code.

mcq.q: How many bits are needed for an opcode that must support 64 operations?
mcq.explanation: 2^6 = 64, so 6 bits are needed.

mcq.q: In the expression 2 + 3, the numbers 2 and 3 are called:
mcq.explanation: Operands are the data on which the operation works.

mcq.q: Program Counter (PC) in a basic computer is how many bits?
mcq.explanation: PC is 12 bits, because memory has 4096 (2^12) addresses.

mcq.q: The Instruction Register (IR) is:
mcq.explanation: IR is 16 bits and stores the instruction being executed.

mcq.q: Memory size of a basic computer is:
mcq.explanation: 4096 words, each word 16 bits.

mcq.q: Which register holds the result of arithmetic and logic operations?
mcq.explanation: Accumulator (AC) holds intermediate and final results.

mcq.q: Which register holds characters given by the user?
mcq.explanation: INPR (Input Register) holds input characters.

mcq.q: The Address Register (AR) is also known as:
mcq.explanation: AR is also called MAR (Memory Address Register).

mcq.q: Control signal that copies data from the bus into a register is:
mcq.explanation: LD (load) loads the register from the bus.

mcq.q: Control signal that sets register content to zero is:
mcq.explanation: CLR clears the register.

mcq.q: In a common bus system, how many select lines are needed to select one of 8 registers?
mcq.explanation: 2^3 = 8, so 3 select lines (S2, S1, S0).

mcq.q: A bus is:
options: A wire or collection of wires carrying multi-bit information
mcq.explanation: A bus is one or more wires that carry multi-bit information.

mcq.q: In a control word, SELOPR field has how many bits?
mcq.explanation: SELOPR = 5 bits (slide: 3, 3, 5, 3 bits).

mcq.q: Total number of bits in the control word (SELA, SELB, SELD, SELOPR) is:
mcq.explanation: 3 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 14 bits (as on the slide).

mcq.q: In the operation R3 = R1 + R2, SELA is set to:
mcq.explanation: SELA = 001 places R1 on bus A.

mcq.q: Micro-operation 'Complement A' is coded as:
mcq.explanation: 01000 = Complement A (COMA).

mcq.q: A stack follows which order?
mcq.explanation: Stack is LIFO (Last In First Out).

mcq.q: PUSH operation in a stack:
mcq.explanation: PUSH inserts an item on the top of the stack.

mcq.q: Which register points to the top of the stack?
mcq.explanation: Stack Pointer (SP) holds the address of the top item.

mcq.q: Postfix expression 3 4 * 5 6 * + evaluates to:
Which is NOT one of the three segments of computer memory partitioned for stack usage?
mcq.explanation: The three segments are Program, Data and Stack.

mcq.q: Which instruction format is most commonly used?
mcq.explanation: Two address format is the most commonly used.

mcq.q: Which format uses the stack for all operands?
mcq.explanation: Zero address format uses a stack; there is no address field.

mcq.q: One-address format uses which special instructions?
mcq.explanation: One address instructions use LOAD and STORE with the accumulator.

mcq.q: Three address format requires:
options: Shorter programs but more bits per instruction
mcq.explanation: It uses more bits but produces shorter assembly programs.

mcq.q: In direct addressing mode, the address field contains:
mcq.explanation: Direct addressing: the address field gives the operand's effective address.

mcq.q: In immediate addressing mode, the operand is:
mcq.explanation: Immediate addressing: the operand is given directly in the instruction.

mcq.q: Register direct addressing requires how many memory references to fetch the operand?
mcq.explanation: The operand is in a register, so no memory reference is needed.

mcq.q: Register indirect addressing requires how many memory references?
mcq.explanation: Only one memory reference is needed to fetch the operand.

mcq.q: Instruction 'CMA' (complement accumulator) uses which addressing mode?
mcq.explanation: Operand is implied (accumulator), so it is implied mode.

mcq.q: Accumulator in the basic computer is how many bits?
mcq.explanation: AC is 16 bits.

mcq.q: The memory address register (AR) is how many bits?
mcq.explanation: AR is 12 bits.

mcq.q: When the stack pointer becomes 0 after a POP, the stack is:
mcq.explanation: Per the stack algorithm, SP = 0 after a POP means the stack is EMPTY.

mcq.q: Zero address instructions are called stack-based because:
options: They have no address field and use the stack
mcq.explanation: No address field: operands are taken from the stack.

mcq.q: According to the slide, the SELOPR field of the control word has how many bits?
mcq.explanation: SELOPR is 5 bits. The total control word is 14 bits.

mcq.q: In the two-address example for (A+B)*(C+D), the first instruction is:
mcq.explanation: The sequence starts with MOV R1, A, then ADD R1, B.

mcq.q: For the instruction ADD 300 with memory[300] = 1350, the operand is found at:
mcq.explanation: Indirect mode: address 300 holds the operand address 1350.

mcq.q: In ADD 10 (immediate mode), the value 10 is:
mcq.explanation: Immediate mode: the operand is the value given in the instruction.

mcq.q: Postfix form of A*B + C*D is:
mcq.explanation: Infix A*B + C*D becomes postfix AB* CD* +.

mcq.q: A memory stack example has program segment at 1000, operands at 2000 and stack starting at:
mcq.explanation: The slide shows the stack at 3000.

short.q: Define an instruction code and state its two parts.
short.answer: An instruction code is a group of bits that tells the computer to perform a specific operation. It has two parts: opcode (operation) and operand (data or address).

short.q: What is an operand? Give an example.
short.answer: An operand is the data or address part of an instruction on which the operation is done. Example: in 2 + 3, 2 and 3 are operands.

short.q: What is the role of the Program Counter (PC)?
short.answer: PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched from memory after the current instruction is completed. It is 12 bits.

short.q: Give the sizes of the Accumulator, Input register and Output register in a basic computer.
short.answer: AC is 16 bits, INPR is 8 bits, OUTR is 8 bits.

short.q: What is the function of the Data Register (DR)?
short.answer: DR (also called MDR) holds memory operands; data fetched from memory is stored here for processing (16 bits).

short.q: Name the three control signals used with registers and state what each does.
short.answer: LD (load): copies data from the bus into the register. INR (increment): increases the register content by one. CLR (clear): sets the register content to zero.

short.q: What is a common bus system?
short.answer: It is a system in which all registers are connected to a shared bus. Select lines choose which register puts its data on the bus, so only one register uses the bus at a time.

short.q: How many select lines are needed to choose one of 8 registers on the common bus?
short.answer: 3 select lines (S2, S1, S0), because 2^3 = 8.

short.q: What is a micro-operation? Name any three.
short.answer: A micro-operation is a basic operation on data in registers, performed in one clock cycle. Examples: transfer, increment, AND, complement, shift (any three).

short.q: Explain the four fields of a control word.
short.answer: SELA (3 bits) selects the register for bus A; SELB (3 bits) selects the register for bus B; SELD/SELREG (3 bits) selects the destination register; SELOPR (5 bits) selects the ALU operation.

short.q: Give the selection bits to perform R3 = R1 + R2.
short.answer: SELA = 001 (R1), SELB = 010 (R2), SELOPR = 10010 (ADD), SELD = 011 (R3).

short.q: What is a stack and what does LIFO mean?
short.answer: A stack is a data structure where the item stored last is retrieved first. LIFO = Last In, First Out.

short.q: Explain the PUSH and POP operations of a stack.
short.answer: PUSH inserts an item at the top: SP <- SP + 1, M[SP] <- DR. POP removes the top item: DR <- M[SP], SP <- SP - 1.

short.q: What is the role of the stack pointer?
short.answer: The stack pointer (SP) is a register that holds the address of the item on the top of the stack, and it changes on each push and pop.

short.q: Evaluate the postfix expression 3 4 * 5 6 * + using a stack.
short.answer: Push 3, push 4, multiply -> 12; push 5, push 6, multiply -> 30; add -> 42.

short.q: Differentiate between three-address and two-address instruction formats.
short.answer: Three address has three operand fields (shorter programs, more bits per instruction). Two address has two operand fields and is the most commonly used format.

short.q: What is a zero address instruction format?
short.answer: An instruction format with no address field; the operands are taken from the stack (stack-based computers).

short.q: What are LOAD and STORE instructions? In which format are they used?
short.answer: LOAD brings an operand from memory into the accumulator; STORE saves the accumulator content into memory. They are used in the one address instruction format.

short.q: What is addressing mode? Explain direct addressing with an example.
short.answer: Addressing mode is the technique for specifying the address of the operand. In direct addressing the address field contains the effective address of the operand. Example: ADD 547 uses the data at memory location 547.

short.q: Explain indirect addressing mode.
short.answer: The address field points to a memory word that contains the address of the operand. It needs two memory references (one for the pointer, one for the operand).

short.q: Differentiate between immediate and register addressing modes.
short.answer: Immediate: operand is inside the instruction itself. Register: operand is in a CPU register named in the instruction. Neither needs a memory reference for the operand itself, but register mode is named in the register.

short.q: What is register indirect addressing mode?
short.answer: The register contains the address of the operand in memory. Only one memory reference is required to fetch the operand.

short.q: Give an example of implied addressing mode.
short.answer: CMA (Complement Accumulator): the operand (accumulator) is implied by the instruction, so no address is written.

short.q: Write the one-address (LOAD/STORE) instructions to compute (A+B)*(C+D).
short.answer: LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X.

short.q: Explain indirect addressing with the example ADD 300 where memory[300] = 1350.
short.answer: The address field 300 holds the address of a memory word; that word contains 1350, the address of the operand. So the operand is read from 1350 (two memory references).
